name: T3 / thyroid fat loss

lead: T3 is the active thyroid hormone, available by prescription as liothyronine for hypothyroidism. In bodybuilding and cutting circles it has been used off-label to raise metabolic rate and lose body fat for a leaner look.

T3 raises basal metabolic rate, affects protein synthesis and increases sensitivity to catecholamines such as adrenaline. The prescribing label states that in people with normal thyroid function, ordinary hormone-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses can cause serious toxicity. No published trial of T3 as a cosmetic fat-loss method was found.

paras: Use is described mainly in bodybuilding contexts during short cutting phases, alongside calorie restriction and training, and usually discussed as a prescription-only drug obtained through a clinician. Reported timelines are weeks.

Excess thyroid hormone can cause sweating, tremor, insomnia, arrhythmias and heart failure. The label warns of serious or life-threatening toxicity at larger doses, especially alongside sympathomimetic amines. It can also suppress the body's own thyroid function. It is prescription-only in the UK and Canada.

angle.text: Users take the thyroid hormone T3 off-label during cutting phases to raise metabolic rate and shed body fat for a leaner look. The drug is approved for hypothyroidism, and its label states that normal-range doses are ineffective for weight reduction in people with normal thyroid function.

lead: Liothyronine is a synthetic form of triiodothyronine (T3), the more active of the two main thyroid hormones. It was approved for medical use in 1956 and is prescribed mainly for hypothyroidism and myxedema coma.[1][1]

In bodybuilding and physique circles, T3 (often by its brand name Cytomel) is taken off-label during a cut with the aim of a leaner, more defined look: the idea is that thyroid hormone raises basal metabolic rate and fat oxidation, so more body fat is lost while dieting.[2][3] Wikipedia's article on T3 confirms that the hormone increases basal metabolic rate and stimulates lipid breakdown.[2] Physique forums also discuss thyroid markers such as free T3 and reverse T3 as a way of understanding fatigue and metabolic slowdown on a long diet.[4][5]

The prescribing information for liothyronine states that in people with normal thyroid function, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction and that larger doses can be seriously toxic.[1] The American Thyroid Association says the only safety concerns of thyroid hormone are taking too much or too little.[6] Competition rules for some natural bodybuilding federations list T3 and T4 among prohibited substances.[7]

Related thyroid preparations have a long history in weight discussions. Desiccated thyroid extract, made from animal glands, was first used for myxedema in 1891 and later became a commercial product, and in the 1970s better assays showed it produced supraphysiologic T3 levels. [8] The American Thyroid Association says thyroid hormone has been used for weight loss in the past but that taking extra raises the risk of serious side effects, including palpitations, insomnia, anxiety and loss of muscle and bone mass, and that weight lost this way usually returns when the extra hormone is stopped. [9]
infobox: T3 isolated 1948 (Melbourne); identified in human plasma 1952 [2]

paras: Liothyronine is prescribed for hypothyroidism and myxedema coma, and may be considered where peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 is poor. It has also been used in thyroid cancer care and as an add-on to some antidepressants.[1] Because of its fast onset and short half-life, it is useful when a short withdrawal period is wanted before radioactive iodine therapy for thyroid cancer.[1]

A network meta-analysis of augmentation strategies for treatment-resistant depression, covering 65 studies and 12,415 patients, reported that liothyronine was among agents with significantly better response rates than placebo.[10] The American Thyroid Association states that there is no indication for T3 alone in treating hypothyroidism, while some patients may try adding T3 to T4 for 3 to 6 months.[6] Roughly 25 micrograms of liothyronine corresponds to 100 micrograms of levothyroxine.[1]

Liothyronine increases basal metabolic rate, influences protein synthesis and increases sensitivity to catecholamines. It has a faster onset and shorter half-life than levothyroxine.[1] T3 raises oxygen and energy consumption and speeds turnover of macromolecules; for proteins it increases synthesis, though in excess breakdown can outpace it.[2]
The thyroid mainly secretes T4 (levothyroxine); the body converts it to the active T3 as needed. Synthetic T3 acts quickly and wears off fast, so it is dosed differently from T4.[6]

The label lists a half-life of about 2.5 days and high plasma protein binding.[1] Newer formulations such as poly-zinc-liothyronine and sustained-release combinations have been tested in phase 1 and randomized trials aimed at smoothing absorption.[11][12]

sections.h: Use for fat loss in physique culture
paras: A T Nation steroid overview from 2003 lists Cytomel as a synthetic thyroid hormone used by bodybuilders, noting suppression of the body's own thyroid function during use.[3] Participants in T Nation threads discuss thyroid markers such as free T3 and reverse T3 and the fast action of liothyronine compared with levothyroxine.[4][5] Others discuss thyroid lab values while on testosterone therapy and the competitive context in which natural federations restrict thyroid hormones.[7][13]

The product's boxed warning says that doses within the normal daily hormone range are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid people, and that larger doses may produce serious or life-threatening toxicity, particularly when taken with sympathomimetic amines.[1] Use for obesity is not recommended.[1]
Liothyronine is a prescription-only medicine in the UK and Canada.[1]

In 2017 the UK Competition and Markets Authority investigated alleged excessive and unfair pricing by Advanz Pharma; a pack that cost 4.46 pounds before debranding in 2007 was priced at 258.19 pounds by July 2017.[1]
Natural bodybuilding federations may list T3 and T4 among prohibited substances, a topic discussed in physique forums.[7]

Side effects resemble hyperthyroidism and include sweating, nervousness, heat sensitivity and weight loss; less common effects include diarrhea, headache, insomnia, tremor, irritability and menstrual changes. Excess doses can cause arrhythmias and heart failure. It is contraindicated in thyrotoxicosis and uncorrected adrenal insufficiency.[1] The American Thyroid Association adds that excess T3 can cause rapid heartbeat, insomnia and anxiety and may affect the heart and bones.[6]

Wikipedia's account of triiodothyronine says Hird and Trikojus first isolated T3 at the University of Melbourne in 1948, but their paper was little known; Jack Gross and Rosalind Pitt-Rivers are usually credited with identifying T3 in human plasma, publishing in 1952 after Gross joined Pitt-Rivers in London [2]. Synthetic liothyronine was approved for medical use in 1956 [1].

The hormone's effect on energy expenditure has made thyroid preparations a recurring subject in weight-related discussions. Wikipedia describes T3 as roughly four times more potent than T4 at target tissues, with about 85 percent of circulating T3 produced by removal of an iodine atom from T4 in the liver and other tissues [2].

T3 raises basal metabolic rate, increasing oxygen and energy use, and boosts the synthesis and activity of the sodium-potassium ATPase pump, which consumes a large share of cellular energy; it also raises protein and lipid turnover and heart rate and contractility [2]. This is the physiological basis for the physique-culture idea of using the hormone during a cut. The same turnover effect applies to protein, and Wikipedia notes that in excess, protein breakdown can outpace synthesis [2].

Wikipedia's triiodothyronine article does not describe T3 as a weight-loss drug. It notes that T3 alone is not recommended for treating hypothyroidism because it can produce unsafe free T3 levels, that combined T4/T3 therapy is debated, and that related compounds 3,3'-T2 and 3,5-T2, which appear in some over-the-counter bodybuilding supplements, have been studied for fat-related effects in rats [2]. The same page notes that T3 has been used for 'Wilson's syndrome', a diagnosis not recognised by mainstream medicine, and that the American Thyroid Association regards such treatment as potentially harmful [2].

sections.h: Thyroid hormone, dieting and the physique
paras: The appearance rationale rests on the thyroid's control of energy use. Wikipedia describes T3 as raising basal metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, and thyroid hormone is also discussed in relation to adaptation to prolonged calorie restriction, where lower protein turnover may reduce the effects of scarce energy. [2] Physique forum members extend this to dieting: a T Nation author who wrote a thyroid primer says starvation or extremely low-fat diets can raise reverse T3, which they describe as blocking the effect of free T3 and producing hypothyroid-type symptoms even with normal free T3. [4]

The same thread describes low thyroid function as slowing mitochondria so they burn less sugar and fat, and recommends nutrients such as iodine and selenium; the thread is an informal post by a non-medical author, and the claims are those of the poster. [4] On the medical side, the American Thyroid Association says that once thyroid levels are normal the ability to gain or lose weight is the same as in people without thyroid problems, and that hypothyroidism typically causes modest weight gain, mostly water and salt, which treatment generally returns to its prior level. [9]

Federations that run drug-tested natural competitions publish banned lists. A T Nation thread quoting the WNBF banned substance list shows T3 (liothyronine sodium, Cytomel) and T4 (levothyroxine) listed as banned, and describes polygraph and urine testing with a ten-year suspension for a failure. [7] Posters in the thread disagree about how rigorously different leagues test. [7] Competitors who need thyroid hormone for a diagnosed condition are therefore in a regulatory grey area that varies by federation.

Wikipedia notes that two thyronine metabolites, 3,3'-T2 and 3,5-T2, are present in some over-the-counter fat-loss supplements, with the supporting research coming from rat studies of fatty-acid metabolism; it reports no human trial results. [2] Desiccated thyroid extract, a prescription product from animal glands, gives high T3 relative to synthetic T4 and is recommended against for hypothyroidism by the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists and the Royal College of Physicians in favour of levothyroxine. [8] Wikipedia also records that T3 has been used for 'Wilson's syndrome', a diagnosis not recognised by mainstream medicine, and that the American Thyroid Association says such treatment may be harmful. [2]
No studies found on T3 for cosmetic or looksmaxxing fat loss in people with normal thyroid function. Related human research on liothyronine includes the following.

Related reviews and statements. The American Thyroid Association's patient guidance on weight states that extra thyroid hormone raises the risk of serious side effects and that any weight lost generally returns after stopping. [9] The prescribing information's boxed warning states that doses within the daily hormonal range are ineffective for weight reduction in euthyroid people. [1]
Healthy volunteers. A randomized trial examined the acute effects of liothyronine on the cardiovascular system and energy metabolism in healthy volunteers.[14]

Hypothyroidism. A randomized double-blind crossover study of 75 hypothyroid patients compared levothyroxine, desiccated thyroid extract and levothyroxine plus liothyronine, and a 2025 feasibility trial compared levothyroxine with the combination after thyroid surgery.[15][16] Earlier studies of combination therapy did not find consistent superiority of one treatment over another.[15] The American Thyroid Association's 2014 hypothyroidism guidelines address replacement therapy.[17]
Depression. The network meta-analysis above found liothyronine augmentation associated with better response rates than placebo.[10]

lore.intro: T3 comes up in bodybuilding forums as a cutting aid, in natural-federation rule discussions, and in threads about thyroid lab values and diet-related thyroid slowdown.[3][4][7]
